executive_summary: EUR/CAD trades at 1.62394 (5 August close), up 1.12% over one month, 0.94% over three months, 1.71% over six months and just 0.21% over twelve — a pair that has gone almost nowhere in a year while travelling a great deal, having collapsed 5.6% from 1.64672 (17 October 2025) to 1.554 (15 March 2026) before grinding back to the 75th percentile of its 52-week range. The dominant bilateral narrative is a genuine curiosity: this is the only zero-carry pair in the G10, with the ECB deposit rate and the Bank of Canada overnight target both at exactly 2.25%, which strips out the funding channel entirely and makes EUR/CAD the cleanest available expression of relative fundamentals — and relative fundamentals are pulling in opposite directions on different clocks. Three bilateral differentials diverge materially from what either standalone dossier implies. First, the policy differential is zero today but the ECB has a 77–83% priced hike on 10 September against a Bank of Canada the market has flat until March 2027, giving EUR/CAD the largest available swing in relative carry from a standing start anywhere in the complex — potentially 0bp to +50bp by year-end. Second, that same energy shock which underwrites the ECB's hawkishness is a direct terms-of-trade transfer from the euro area to Canada: Brent at $90–92 and TTF at €58.62/MWh (+66% y/y) simultaneously tax a euro area whose goods balance has swung €22.8bn into deficit and subsidise a Canada printing record C$77.1bn export months — the rate benefit and the external cost share one cause, and bilaterally they very nearly cancel. Third, positioning is short both legs, but proportionally the Canadian dollar short is roughly four times more crowded (27.5% of open interest versus 7.1%), while the real-money book — asset managers long 228,927 EUR contracts and short 101,160 CAD contracts — is implicitly a large long EUR/CAD position that constitutes a strategic supply overhang. We are tactically Bullish at conviction 2 (weighted score +0.1022, barely clear of the Neutral band), targeting 1.6320 into the 10 September ECB meeting on the back of the 19 August Section 338 tariff cliff and an ECB-first event sequence; strategically Neutral at conviction 2 (weighted score −0.0130), because the energy transfer and Canada's vastly superior fiscal position offset the rate trajectory once the September hike is banked. The caveat is that the tactical edge is thin, dated and expires in mid-September; this is a time-boxed trade, not a position.

market_context.valuation_assessment: There is no pair-level PPP series available, so the bilateral valuation is constructed from the two BIS real broad effective exchange rates: the euro area at 102.69 (June 2026, 0.5% above its 30-month mean, down 1.2% y/y) against Canada at 95.71 (June 2026, the lowest print in its retrieved series, down 3.4% y/y and 2.1% m/m). On a relative real-effective basis the euro is therefore approximately 3.3% rich to the Canadian dollar, implying a fair value near EUR/CAD 1.5653 against spot 1.62394. Canada is one of only two G10 real exchange rates below 100 and sits near a decade low while the euro sits fractionally above its own mean; on the valuation channel alone the pair should be lower, and it has instead risen 1.7% over six months. Historical percentile is not computable from a 30-month BIS window and is not asserted. The practical reading is that valuation is a strategic drag on a long EUR/CAD position worth roughly 3–4% of notional if it ever mean-reverts, and it is one of the two anchors (with terms of trade) holding the strategic stance at Neutral rather than Bullish.

market_context.recent_regime: The regime since mid-July has been a quiet, grinding recovery in EUR/CAD from 1.59935 (19 July) to 1.62411 (5 August), a 1.5% advance over thirteen sessions on progressively smaller daily ranges — the signature of a positioning-and-carry drift rather than a news-driven repricing. The dominant narrative is the failure of the oil channel: Brent rose roughly 26–31% through July and the Canadian dollar captured almost none of it, because the shock transmitted into US term premium rather than Canadian yields, so a pair that should mechanically have fallen on a commodity impulse instead rose. Layered on that is an event asymmetry that neither dossier frames bilaterally: the euro area secured a 15% US tariff ceiling effective 1 July while Canada's USMCA was not renewed on the same date and now faces 50% Section 338 duties from around 19 August. The tension to resolve over the next six months is whether the euro area's rate trajectory can outrun a terms-of-trade transfer flowing directly to Canada.

bilateral_carry_analysis.carry_assessment: EUR/CAD is the only pair in the G10+SGD complex with an exactly zero policy-rate differential — ECB deposit at 2.25% and BoC overnight target at 2.25%. At overnight fixings the picture tilts marginally against a long EUR/CAD (€STR 2.185% vs CORRA 2.31%, −12.5bp annualised), and further out the curve the Canadian dollar is paid more despite identical policy rates (2yr −9bp, 10yr −44bp against the euro), reflecting Canada's larger term premium and issuance profile. Carry is emphatically working in the current low-volatility environment across G10 generally, but EUR/CAD is the one pair where that regime has no purchase because there is nothing to earn or pay. The practical consequence is that this cross is a pure directional and relative-fundamentals expression: neither leg is a funding currency against the other, no carry-trade community exists in this pair, and a position can be held indefinitely at negligible cost — which removes the tailwind that sustains crowded shorts elsewhere but also removes the bleed that forces early exit from a wrong view. The sign flip in the computed forward curve across tenors (+1.7 pips at 1M to −11.7 pips at 6M) is unique to this pair and confirms the market is pricing the policy differential moving from marginally against the euro at one month to marginally in the euro's favour at six months, at exactly the size the differential implies and no more.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The differential is exactly zero — 2.25% against 2.25% — and the trajectory is unambiguously widening in the euro's favour, with market-implied probability of a 25bp ECB hike on 10 September running at 76.9% to 83% and a 91.9% cumulative probability that the deposit rate is above 2.25% by 17 December, against a Bank of Canada whose own Market Participants Survey has 2.25% held through July, September, October and December 2026 with no hike until March 2027 and a 2.75% terminal. Bilaterally, that means EUR/CAD is the cross where a September ECB hike creates the largest change in relative carry from a standing start available anywhere in the complex: 0bp becomes +25bp on 10 September and potentially +50bp by 17 December. The pricing problem inside four weeks is that this is already substantially embedded — the computed forward curve flips from +1.7 pips at one month to −11.7 pips at six months precisely because the hike is priced — so the tactical signal is a sequencing signal rather than a mispricing signal. The transmission mechanism is the front end of the two curves: the Schatz at 2.76% already sits 51bp above the €STR fixing while the Government of Canada 2-year at 2.85% sits 60bp above the Bank of Canada target, so on a term-premium-adjusted basis the Canadian front end embeds more tightening risk than the German one, which is the honest counter-argument to a bullish stance. What tips it bullish rather than neutral is the calendar: the Bank of Canada meets on 2 September with a near-certain hold and no projections, and the ECB meets on 10 September with new staff projections in Berlin, so the only meeting inside the window capable of moving the differential moves it in the euro's favour.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the rate channel is the euro's single best bilateral argument and it survives on a real-rate comparison rather than a nominal one. The euro area's 2.25% policy rate against July HICP of 2.9% is a real policy rate of −0.65%; Canada's identical 2.25% against CPI-trim of 1.80% is a real policy rate of +0.45%. The ECB is 110bp further behind its own preferred inflation measure than the Bank of Canada is behind its own, a mechanical reason for the differential to open in the euro's favour irrespective of either central bank's rhetoric. The Bank of Canada is explicitly and publicly pre-committed to inaction on the first round of an oil shock, judging the current rate appropriate with CPI-trim at 1.80% and CPI-median at 1.90% — both below target and lower than May — while the ECB has stated that risks to the inflation outlook are to the upside with core at 2.5% and services at 3.3%. The critical bilateral qualification, and the reason confidence is 55 rather than 70, is that both central banks now have live hawkish repricing paths and Canada's is the one the market has not marked: the 28 October Monetary Policy Report was built on the 9 July futures curve assuming WTI at $65 and Brent near $75 against actuals of $84.25 and $91.82, and Governing Council has published a conditional commitment that a sustained oil increase with broadening spillovers would likely require a monetary policy response. If both banks tighten 25bp by year-end the differential returns to zero and this factor's entire contribution evaporates. The transmission runs through the 2-year spread, currently −9bp against the euro; a 50bp ECB path against a static BoC should take it to roughly +40bp, worth approximately 100–130 pips on the cross.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: This is the clearest example in the pair of two reinforcing standalone views cancelling bilaterally. The euro dossier scores its own Factor 2 tactically Bullish at 60 on a July data cluster in which flash HICP accelerated on all four relevant components — headline 2.9%, core 2.5%, services 3.3%, energy 10.0% — alongside a Q2 GDP beat of +0.4% q/q against 0.2% consensus and a composite PMI at a five-month high of 51.9. The Canadian dossier scores its own Factor 2 tactically Bullish at 58 on an equally genuine inflection: monthly GDP +0.3% in May with a +0.2% June advance implying roughly +0.8% q/q in Q2 after 0.0% in Q1, unemployment down for a second consecutive month to 6.5%, wages accelerating to 3.3% and record retail sales of C$73.7bn. Both economies are surprising to the upside simultaneously, so the pair signal is close to nil. The one durable bilateral asymmetry is compositional: the euro area's inflation is above target and broadening into core and services while Canada's preferred cores are below target and falling, which gives the euro the policy-relevant differential of +70bp on core even as Canada holds the growth-momentum differential. Asymmetric sensitivity matters here: the pair is more likely to move on Canadian releases than euro-area ones inside four weeks, because the 7 August Labour Force Survey, 17 August CPI and 28 August Q2 GDP are all higher-variance events than anything on the European calendar before 1 September, and all three carry upside risk that would push the pair lower.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Strategically the compositional asymmetry becomes the whole story and it favours a rising pair, but weakly. The euro area's core HICPX is projected to peak at 2.7% in early 2027 with headline peaking at 3.4% in Q3–Q4 2026, while the Bank of Canada projects its trim/median core average at exactly 2.0% through Q4-2026 and headline back at 2% in early 2027 — a persistent core differential of roughly 50–70bp in the euro's favour across the horizon. Growth forecasts, by contrast, are almost identical: the ECB projects euro-area GDP at 0.8% in 2026 rising to 1.8% in 2027, while the Bank of Canada projects 0.7% in 2026 rising to 1.8% in 2027, as close to a bilateral wash as two forecasts can be. Two offsetting risks keep confidence at 52. First, the euro area's inflation impulse is cost-push and self-liquidating without second-round effects, and there are none — the ECB wage tracker sits at 2.3% for 2026 and 2.7% for Q1-2027. Second, Canada's inflation has a live upside path the euro area's does not: the Bank estimates war-related cost pressures peaking at 0.4 percentage points on headline CPI in Q1-2027, and Q2 business survey respondents already expect 3.0–3.5% inflation over one and two years, rising specifically on oil. If Canadian cores converge up to 2.3–2.5% while euro-area cores decay to 2.3%, the differential closes and this factor turns Neutral. On balance the euro retains the core gap and the pair retains a modest upward bias.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: EUR/CAD belongs firmly in the low risk-sensitivity category, and the current regime confirms it. Neither leg is a safe haven — the euro weakens in severe risk-off as capital moves to the dollar, franc and yen, while Canada weakens against the US dollar in risk-off but strengthens against higher-beta commodity currencies. The two legs therefore behave similarly in most risk states, which is why the pair's realised correlation to global equities is weak and why a record global risk rally has produced only a 1.12% one-month move in the cross. The bilateral distinction that does exist runs marginally in the euro's favour in stress and marginally in Canada's favour in benign conditions: the euro is the mechanical anti-dollar with a 57.6% DXY weight and gains in a broad dollar decline, while Canada's economy is anchored to US demand with roughly 75% of goods exports going to a single partner, making the Canadian dollar quasi-dollar-bloc and therefore a lower-beta recipient of any dollar move. In the current environment — VIX 17.09, US investment-grade OAS 80–81bp, high-yield 281–284bp, STOXX Europe 600 at a record 655.45 — both currencies are receiving mild support and the net is close to nil. The one live bilateral asymmetry is that the euro is used as a funding currency in a sustained risk-on regime, which mechanically sells euros; but EUR/CAD is precisely the pair where that mechanism has no purchase, because the Canadian dollar offers no yield pickup over the euro to fund into.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Both legs are net short and the bilateral question is which short is more extreme relative to its own market, because that determines where the larger latent squeeze sits. On absolute notional the two are close — leveraged funds short 56,671 EURO FX contracts (approximately $8.2bn) against 102,495 Canadian dollar contracts (approximately $7.4bn) — which would imply a muted pair signal. Proportionally they are not close at all: the euro short is 7.1% of 800,061 lots of open interest while the Canadian short is 27.5% of 372,447 lots, so the Canadian dollar short is roughly 3.9 times more crowded relative to the market that must absorb its unwind. That asymmetry is the tactical signal and it points the pair DOWN: covering 128,886 contracts of gross Canadian short means roughly C$12.9bn of buying into a market where dealers already carry a C$20.6bn long inventory they would be reducing simultaneously, whereas the euro short — though at the 0th percentile of its own 25-week sample — is only about 7–8% of the deepest CME FX contract and has far more depth to absorb it. The historical analogue supports the direction: the 13 August 2024 Canadian record of −103,134 contracts, which the current reading sits 639 contracts inside, preceded a sharp Canadian dollar recovery. The transmission to the cross is direct but imperfect, because both squeezes are expressed against the US dollar rather than against each other, so a simultaneous double squeeze would leave EUR/CAD roughly unchanged; the bearish edge is the differential in squeeze potential, not the existence of squeezes. The counter-argument, and the reason confidence stops at 58, is that the Canadian short is funded at 137.5bp a year against the US dollar and has already survived a 26–31% Brent rally without covering, strong evidence it is a durable rate-differential position rather than a fragile speculative one.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Strategically the fast-money extremes are irrelevant — by definition they resolve inside the tactical window — and the relevant book is real money, where the bilateral read is unambiguous and points the pair lower. Asset managers are net long 228,927 EURO FX contracts and net short 101,160 Canadian dollar contracts, which combines into a very large implicit long EUR/CAD position held by the slowest-moving, least price-sensitive cohort in the market. On the euro side that long is being reduced at roughly 25,800 contracts per four weeks; on the Canadian side the short sits at only about 62% of its own record of −162,229 set on 31 December 2024, so real money retains roughly 61,000 contracts of capacity to add. Both directions of adjustment reduce the implicit long EUR/CAD. The pair-specific interpretation is that EUR/CAD sitting at the 75th percentile of its 52-week range is partly a positioning artefact — the cross has been bought as a by-product of two independent dollar views rather than on its own merits — and the standing supply overhang from a slow real-money reduction is a persistent cap rather than a violent unwind. The offsetting consideration is that this is a slow flow: 20,000–30,000 contracts per month of euro reduction is roughly $3–4bn against average daily turnover in the hundreds of billions, absorbable but directional.

Strategically the fast-money extremes have resolved and the operative book is a real-money position implicitly and heavily long EUR/CAD, reducing on the euro side and with capacity to add on the Canadian side: a persistent cap rather than a squeeze.

tactical.combined_positioning_signal: Fast money is roughly flat the cross (short both legs); aggregate implied EUR/CAD position is long, driven by a real-money book of +228,927 EUR and −101,160 CAD, with no fast-money defence — the least stable configuration available.
tactical.unwind_trigger: Four dated events inside four weeks point in opposite directions: Canadian July CPI (17 August) reversing above 2.0% or Q2 GDP (28 August) confirming +0.8% would force Canadian shorts to cover (bearish pair); Section 338 tariffs taking effect (~19 August) would validate the Canadian short and reward the euro's relative trade-policy certainty (bullish pair).
tactical.historical_analogue: The March 2026 episode, in which EUR/CAD fell 4.8% in eleven sessions from 1.6323 to 1.554 — a move of exactly the character a crowded real-money long unwinding into a thin cross produces, the single best precedent for downside if the current configuration breaks.
tactical.contrarian_case: The aggregate implied pair position is long, held by the slowest cohort, with the more crowded fast-money leg on the quote side. That is the least stable configuration available — a crowded position held by slow capital with no fast capital defending it — and it is the basis for a bearish contrarian read on a pair that otherwise looks tactically bullish on rates and guidance.

strategic.combined_positioning_signal: The stretched book at this horizon is the real-money implicit long EUR/CAD, large in absolute terms but not at a percentile extreme on either leg individually — euro asset managers long but reducing, Canadian asset managers short at only 62% of record. Neither cohort is capitulating.
strategic.unwind_trigger: Not a single event but a sequence: a 28 October Canadian MPR that raises its oil assumption and lifts the 2027 inflation profile, a November French budget episode widening OAT-Bund through 100bp, or a Canadian core inflation print reversing above 2.0%.
strategic.historical_analogue: Real money is long EUR/CAD for a defensible reason — the euro area runs a 1.7% of GDP current-account surplus against Canada's 0.87% deficit — and at zero carry there is no financing pressure forcing an exit, unlike prior positioning-driven unwinds in carry pairs.
strategic.contrarian_case: The implied pair long is a residual with no fast-money defence, but nothing forces its liquidation inside six months. The mechanism is a persistent cap rather than a spike, because real money reduces by selling into strength over weeks rather than capitulating; this is why the strategic score sits at Neutral overall rather than outright Bearish despite the contrarian signal.

factors.weight_adjustment_reason: Energy-importer versus energy-exporter is the dominant bilateral channel: every commodity in the framework's direction rules moves the pair the same way, and the realised July beta of +0.04 against an expected clearly-negative sign is the largest identified mispricing.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: This is the pair's cleanest and largest bilateral differential, and it is unambiguous: the same energy shock is a tax on one leg and a subsidy on the other. The euro area is a large net energy importer whose monthly goods balance recorded a €7.8bn deficit in May 2026 against a €15.0bn surplus a year earlier — a €22.8bn year-on-year deterioration with imports up 10.0% and exports up 0.1% — while its twelve-month current-account surplus narrowed from 2.0% to 1.7% of GDP. Canada is the world's fourth-largest crude exporter and printed a record C$77.1bn monthly goods export in May with a C$4.2bn global surplus and a C$11.6bn bilateral surplus with the United States, the largest since January 2025, on a current account of only −0.87% of GDP. Brent at $90.24–91.82 (+26–31% in July) and TTF at €58.62/MWh (+36% m/m, +66% y/y) simultaneously widen the euro area's import bill and Canada's export receipts. The transmission is a mechanical balance-of-payments flow: every dollar on the barrel is worth roughly C$1.5bn a year to Canadian export revenue at 4.3 MMb/d of exports, while the euro area's energy import bill rises with no offsetting volume response. The reason this is scored Bearish at only 60 rather than 75 is that the transmission has visibly broken: Brent rose 26–31% in July and EUR/CAD rose 1.12%, an implied pair beta to oil of approximately +0.04 against a historical sign that should be firmly negative — Canada cannot ship more barrels (Trans Mountain 85% average utilisation, Enbridge Mainline 95.2%) and sells a discounted heavy barrel, but neither explains a beta of the wrong sign, and that is the mispricing.

If the historical oil beta re-asserts even partially, EUR/CAD has 150–250 pips of downside that no rate differential offsets.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: At an adjusted 0.18 strategic weight this is the heaviest factor in the strategic score after Policy & Rates, and it is the reason the strategic stance is Neutral rather than Bullish. The cumulative balance-of-payments arithmetic runs strongly against the pair. On the euro side, the twelve-month current-account surplus has fallen from €318bn (2.0% of GDP) to €272bn (1.7%) with the goods surplus down from €350bn to €286bn, and the forward-looking picture is worse: EU gas storage is roughly 10 percentage points behind the prior year, the balance-of-summer TTF contract trades €2.68/MWh over Winter 26/27 which disincentivises injection, the refill target has been eased from 90% to 80%, and the full EU ban on Russian LNG imports takes effect at end-2026 — a self-imposed supply cut landing in the same month as constrained Hormuz transit. On the Canadian side, a current account already at only −0.87% of GDP moves toward or through balance if oil holds near current levels, with the Bank of Canada projecting business investment boosted by the oil and gas sector. The bilateral valuation channel reinforces this: Canada's BIS real broad REER at 95.71 is 3.4% below a year ago and among the cheapest in the G10, while the euro's at 102.69 sits fractionally above its own mean — a 3.3% relative real overvaluation of the euro implying fair value near 1.5653. The offsetting considerations are genuine: Canada's export volumes are physically capped, it sells a discounted barrel, roughly 75% of its exports go to a partner now imposing 50% duties, and the euro area retains a structural $16.9bn bilateral goods surplus under a deepening EU-Canada framework. But the direction of the cumulative flow is not in doubt.

factors.horizon_split: Both horizons are Bearish and confidence rises from 60 to 68 as the weight rises from 0.09 to 0.18, because the transmission is cumulative rather than instantaneous. Over four weeks the effect is a monthly trade flow of a few billion euros against enormous FX turnover, and the July evidence is that the market simply ignored it. Over one to six months it is a compounding erosion of the euro area's external surplus into a winter in which European storage is ten percentage points behind and the Russian LNG ban lands, set against a Canadian external position improving from an already-narrow deficit.

Natural gas (TTF) ↑ → −EUR (rule: TTF ↑ → −EUR); Canada is a net gas exporter → mild +CAD; net −2 notches → EUR/CAD FALLS. LNG (JKM) ↑ → negative for the euro area (losing the bidding war for flexible Atlantic cargoes, Asian spot LNG at a $1.09/MMBtu premium to TTF) and mildly positive for Canada as a new Pacific-basin supplier; net −1 to −2 notches → EUR/CAD FALLS. Gold ↑ → +CHF, neutral for both legs. Iron ore ↑ → ++AUD, neutral for both legs. Aggregate net commodity exposure is strongly BEARISH EUR/CAD — there is no commodity in the framework's direction rules whose rise favours the euro against the Canadian dollar.

Realised July transmission was the opposite sign, which is precisely the tactical edge.
net_commodity_exposure.scenario_oil_down_10pct: Brent −10% from $90.24 to $81.22 should correspondingly move EUR/CAD roughly +1.0% to +1.5% higher on normal transmission, easing the euro area's import bill while removing Canada's terms-of-trade support.
net_commodity_exposure.dominant_commodity_driver: Crude oil (Brent/WTI-WCS) is the dominant commodity driver for this pair, given Canada's status as the world's fourth-largest crude exporter and the euro area's large net-importer exposure; natural gas/TTF is the secondary and euro-area-specific channel.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The two central banks are signalling in opposite directions and the sequencing inside the tactical window favours the euro. The ECB's 23 July statement held all three rates but asserted that risks to the inflation outlook are to the upside, with Lagarde disclosing that some governors asked whether a hike should be considered, and the June Account records that the hike was carried by all members with no scenario supporting a 2% deposit rate. The Bank of Canada's 15 July communication went the other way: Governing Council judged the current policy rate appropriate and agreed to look through the direct effects of higher global oil prices, reiterating it would not let higher oil prices lead to persistent inflation. Bilaterally that is a clean guidance divergence favouring a rising pair. The credibility differential is close to nil; both institutions are transparent and have followed through. What decides the tactical stance is the calendar sequence: the Bank of Canada meets first, on 2 September, with a near-certain hold and no Monetary Policy Report, a language event at most; the ECB meets on 10 September with new staff projections hosted by the Bundesbank in Berlin, the only genuine information event of the window. Preceding both, the 27 August publication of the ECB Account of the 23 July meeting will document how many governors pushed for a hike. The tactical constraint, and the reason confidence is 55 rather than 70, is that the ECB's hawkishness is fully priced at 77–83% and can only disappoint, while the Bank of Canada's dovishness is fully priced and can only surprise hawkishly.

tactical.what_is_priced: The market prices the ECB as a credible hiker and the Bank of Canada as credibly patient, and both readings are correct. The bilateral asymmetry is in the calendar rather than the content: the euro has a projection round inside the window and Canada does not.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the guidance divergence inverts and cancels, the single most important sequencing insight in this analysis. The euro's guidance advantage is front-loaded: the 10 September projection round is the point of maximum hawkish risk, with 2026 HICP potentially revised toward 3.2% while 2027 stays at or above 2.3%, and the 17 December Eurosystem round follows. But the Canadian guidance event is larger in information content and lands on 28 October, a day before the ECB's own non-projection October meeting. The July Canadian MPR was built on the 9 July oil futures curve and assumes Brent near $75 in Q3-2026 settling toward $70, WTI stabilising at $65 and WCS at $50, against actuals of $91.82 and $84.25 — assumptions roughly $17–19 stale in the inflationary direction. Governing Council has published a conditional commitment that a sustained oil increase with broadening spillovers would likely require a monetary policy response. A credible central bank cannot raise its oil path by $17 and simultaneously ignore its own stated trigger, making 28 October the most underpriced scheduled guidance event affecting this cross — and it is bearish for the pair. Partially offsetting, the same MPR must revise its growth forecast down, because its tariff assumption of a 5.0% average US rate on Canada predates the 20 July Section 338 proclamation entirely, making 28 October a two-sided event. Both banks have embedded a weaker own currency than spot in their projections, so neither has an institutional interest in defending its currency. Net: the euro's guidance edge is real but expires in September; Canada's is dated, larger and lands in October. Neutral.

That asymmetry is the strategic mispricing and it runs against the pair: the euro's guidance edge is banked by mid-September, while the Canadian revision that could close the entire policy differential is unpriced and dated 28 October.

factors.horizon_split: The stance moves from Bullish tactically to Neutral strategically for a purely mechanical, calendar-driven reason. Inside four weeks the only projection round belongs to the ECB. Over one to six months the Bank of Canada acquires the larger and more underpriced event — a 28 October MPR that must revise a $17-stale oil assumption against a published hawkish trigger — and that offsets the euro's September advantage almost exactly. Confidence falls from 55 to 50 because the strategic conclusion depends on judging which of two credible hawkish repricings is larger, and the honest answer is that they are close.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The bilateral event asymmetry inside four weeks is the sharpest of any factor and it is a trade-policy asymmetry that neither standalone dossier frames as a relative story. On 1 July 2026 the EU-US arrangement took effect capping most EU goods at 15% and cutting autos from 27.5% to 15%, and the United States declined to renew the USMCA, leaving the agreement in force only pending resolution or termination. Three weeks later, on 20 July, three presidential proclamations imposed 50% Section 338 tariffs on Canadian motor vehicles, alcoholic beverages and dairy — roughly $20bn of trade — effective approximately 19 August 2026, and critically these apply regardless of whether a good originates under the USMCA. Both economies are heavily exposed to US demand (euro area 21.0% of exports; Canada roughly 75% of goods exports), but only one now has legal certainty about the tariff it faces. Canada has announced no retaliation. The transmission to the cross is direct: a 50% duty on $20bn of Canadian exports with no offsetting measure and no USMCA protection is a Canada-specific negative with a hard date inside the tactical window, and the euro area's equivalent risk — a threatened Section 301 action over EU technology fines — has no date before roughly 21 September. The reason confidence is 58 rather than 70 is that the market has already declined to price this: USD/CAD moved less than a figure across the week of the proclamation.

The bilateral edge is that only one of these has an unconditional legal instrument with a date inside the window, and the pair carries no premium for it.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the event calendar densifies on both sides and the balance tips against the pair, though only marginally and with low confidence. On the euro side the dated risks are unusually specific and large: the French PLF 2027 sequence runs from the 30 September Conseil des ministres through the 20 October vote on Part I to the 17 November solemn vote on the whole bill, with a censure-and-dissolution path assessed at 20–25% probability that would take OAT-Bund from 82bp toward 130bp; four French rating reviews fall between 28 August and 27 November; German state elections on 20 September test the Merz coalition; the Google DMA compliance deadline around 21 September is the most likely trigger for a US Section 301 action against the EU; and the full EU ban on Russian LNG imports takes effect at end-2026. On the Canadian side the risk is one open-ended question — USMCA renewal — plus possible broadening of Section 338 to auto parts or lumber, against a credible negotiated-withdrawal path evidenced by the February 2026 IEEPA reversal. Bilaterally, the euro area's dated calendar is denser, more specific and more consequential over six months than Canada's, a reversal of the tactical position. One structural point cuts mildly the other way: Canada and the EU have both expressed a desire for deeper economic cooperation and enhanced CETA investor-protection/dispute-resolution provisions, reducing bilateral rupture tail risk to essentially zero; there is no trade dispute, sanctions issue or diplomatic tension between these two economies — all the event risk is third-party.

The strategic mispricing is that the euro area's calendar contains three independent, dated, high-impact items in November and December with essentially no premium attached.

factors.horizon_split: The stance flips from Bullish tactically to Bearish strategically because the two calendars are back-loaded differently. Inside four weeks the only unconditional dated instrument is the 19 August Canadian tariff, pair-positive and unpriced. Over one to six months the euro area accumulates a denser and more consequential calendar while Canada's single risk carries a demonstrated reversal precedent. Confidence falls from 58 to 48 because the strategic conclusion requires weighing a French political tail against a Canadian trade tail, and the weighting is genuinely uncertain.

factors.weight_adjustment_reason: A 47.7-percentage-point debt differential (Canada 41.2% vs euro area 88.9%) with a dated binary (17 November French PLF vote) on the weaker leg and no Canadian equivalent. Materially more relevant than the boilerplate this factor usually is.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The fiscal differential between these two sovereigns is the widest of any factor in this analysis and it favours the Canadian dollar decisively. Canada carries federal debt of C$1,266.5bn or 41.2% of GDP with projected deficits of 2.1% and 1.9% of GDP, and is rated Aaa by Moody's, AAA by S&P, AAA by DBRS and AA+ by Fitch, all stable, with no rating action since 2020. The euro area has no single sovereign; aggregate gross government debt is 88.9% of GDP and rising, France carries 117.5% debt with a 5.1% deficit and is rated Aa3 negative by Moody's, and the OAT-Bund spread at 81–82bp now trades at or through the BTP-Bund spread of 80–81bp, an inversion of the euro area's historical credit hierarchy. Bilaterally, that is a 47.7-percentage-point debt differential and a ratings gap of several notches at the weakest euro-area sovereign. The transmission is not immediate — nobody trades EUR/CAD on debt ratios — but it operates through the term premium: the Government of Canada 10-year at 3.59% yields 44bp more than the Bund at 3.15% despite identical policy rates. Inside four weeks nothing is dated: the French budget process does not begin until 30 September, the first French rating review is Fitch on 28 August, and Canada's Budget 2026 has no announced date. The stance is Bearish because the level of the differential is large and the direction of travel is adverse for the euro, but confidence is only 48 because the tactical calendar is empty.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months this factor becomes materially tradeable in the cross and it is the second-largest strategic negative after terms of trade, which is why the weight was raised to 0.09. The French PLF 2027 sequence runs 30 September, 20 October and 17 November, with a Bercy-commissioned report warning the deficit could reach 5.9% of GDP in 2027 and drift to 6.8% by 2030, and a 2026 budget precedent in which Article 49.3 was invoked and censure motions survived. We assess the censure-and-dissolution path at 20–25%, which would take OAT-Bund from 82bp through 130bp and drag the euro 1.0–1.5% lower independently of the ECB. Layered on that is supply: Germany has revised 2026 issuance up to roughly €521.5bn and the EU will issue a record €180bn of joint borrowing, against a Canadian programme funding a 1.9%-of-GDP deficit with three AAA ratings and orderly routine debt management. The bilateral asymmetry is total: Canada has ample fiscal space to respond to the Section 338 tariffs without threatening its credit, while France has none. The one counter-argument is the paradox the Canadian dossier itself identifies: Canada's fiscal strength is why its yields are low, and low yields are why the Canadian dollar has no carry advantage. But at a six-month horizon, with a dated French binary and no dated Canadian equivalent, the differential is a clear negative for the pair.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The pair's own chart is the most straightforwardly bullish input in this analysis, and it is the only factor where the price data and web-based chart work agree without qualification. The moving-average configuration from the 390-day series is cleanly stacked bullish: spot 1.62394 above the 50-day SMA at 1.61503, above the 100-day at 1.61046, above the 200-day at 1.60774, with all three rising and spot 0.55% and 1.01% above the 50- and 200-day respectively. That is a trend regime in which systematic and CTA capital is a buyer rather than a neutral. The structure since 15 March is a sequence of higher lows (1.554 → 1.59187 → 1.59935) and spot has just broken to a five-week high, clearing the 1.6230 pullback resistance identified 31 July as the first upside objective on a break above the 1.61728 pivot. The offsetting facts, and the reason confidence is 55 rather than 70, are position-in-range and volatility. Spot sits at the 75th percentile of a 52-week range whose top at 1.64672 is only 228 pips away, and the pair has made three progressively lower highs since October 2025, so the wedge is compressing. On volatility, 20-day realised computed from the provided series is approximately 3.5% annualised against an estimated 1M implied of 5.5–6.0 — a variance risk premium of roughly +2.0 to +2.5 vols, meaning options are rich to realised and a directional view is more efficiently held in spot than in premium.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Strategically the structure constrains rather than directs, and it constrains in the pair's own favour only if it can break a ceiling it has failed three times. The 52-week range of 1.554–1.64672 has contained the pair through an oil collapse, a 26–31% oil rally, a failed USMCA review, a 50% tariff proclamation, an ECB hike and a hawkish Fed hold — an unusually wide set of shocks absorbed without a range break, strong evidence the range is structurally robust. Spot at the 75th percentile means the strategic bull case requires clearing 1.64672 while the bear case has 698 pips of room before testing the low, an asymmetry of available space rather than probability. The three progressively lower highs since October 2025 against three progressively higher lows describe a compressing wedge that must resolve inside the strategic horizon, and wedges of this shape resolve in the direction of the longer-term trend, which for this pair over one year is flat. On volatility the strategic read is genuinely informative: 20-day realised at 3.5% is exceptionally low in absolute terms while the pair demonstrated in March that it can travel 4.8% in eleven sessions, so the ratio of realised-to-potential volatility is as stretched as it gets. If the estimated term structure in mild contango is right, the market charges no premium for the 28 October Canadian MPR, the 17 November French vote or the end-2026 Russian LNG ban, all inside the three-to-six-month tenor — making longer-dated optionality the strategically attractive expression and a directional spot position the unattractive one.

On the strategic leg, selling the six-month forward at 1.62277 against an expected 1.6200 earns approximately 28 pips; the larger payoff is in volatility, where an estimated 3M implied of 6.0–6.5 embeds no premium for the 28 October Canadian MPR, the 17 November French vote or the end-December Russian LNG ban.
consensus_divergence.risk_if_wrong: If the consensus is right and EUR/CAD reaches 1.60 by Q4-2026, a long position from 1.62394 loses approximately 240 pips (−1.5%); the scenarios that make consensus right are a hawkish 28 October Canadian MPR closing the differential and a sustained oil bid restoring the commodity channel's normal sign, assigned a combined probability of roughly 25%, exactly the weight on the strategic downside case.

cross_horizon_consistency.explanation: The 0.1152-point gap is genuine and mechanical rather than a hedge, almost entirely attributable to weight migration acting on an unchanged set of factor readings. Inflation & Growth falls from 0.18 to 0.10 and Flows & Positioning from 0.12 to 0.07, while External Balance rises from 0.09 to 0.18 (doubling the largest negative) and Fiscal rises from 0.04 to 0.09. Guidance & Credibility switches from Bullish to Neutral and contributes +0.0385 tactically but nothing strategically. Substantively, the tactical case rests on two things with short half-lives — a calendar in which the ECB's only projection round and Canada's only unconditional tariff date both fall inside four weeks — while the strategic case must contend with an energy transfer, a 47.7-percentage-point debt differential and a French budget calendar that only get heavier with time.
cross_horizon_consistency.inflection_point: The window between 10 September and 28 October 2026. The 10 September ECB decision and staff projections is the moment the tactical thesis is either delivered or invalidated (a delivered 77–83%-priced hike is a classic sell-the-fact). From 30 September the French PLF 2027 process takes over as the dominant euro-specific narrative, and on 28 October the Bank of Canada must publish a Monetary Policy Report reconciling a $65 WTI assumption with an $84 market against its own published hawkish trigger. A secondary transition marker is the 1 November EU gas storage reading — below 75% and Factor 5 moves from Bearish 68 toward Bearish 80.
cross_horizon_consistency.trading_implication: The position must be time-boxed, not held open-endedly, and the zero-carry characteristic of this pair makes that discipline cheaper to maintain than in any other euro cross. The tactical long should be sized for a four-week hold with a hard invalidation at a daily close below 1.6088, reduced into rather than held through the 10 September decision. The strategic view is not a spot view at all — with a probability-weighted expected value of −52 pips gross and −62 pips net, there is no directional trade, and the exploitable strategic position is long three-to-six-month volatility, where the market charges nothing for the October–December event cluster.

catalysts.rationale: EUR/CAD is a non-USD cross, so a US payroll surprise transmits through both legs simultaneously and largely cancels — but not entirely. A weak print that undercuts the FOMC's three hike-dissenters would soften the dollar broadly, and the euro captures 57.6% of any DXY move against Canada's quasi-dollar-bloc participation, so the pair rises modestly. Canada's own July Labour Force Survey is released the same day, making this the cleanest relative-data event of the month for the quote leg.

The July Outlook was finalised on 1 July before the Hormuz re-escalation and forecast Brent at $74 in Q3-2026 and $65 in 2027, roughly $18 below spot. The August issue is the first to incorporate the re-escalation and is likely to revise the path materially higher. Under the framework's direction rules an upward oil revision is ++CAD and −EUR, so the pair falls; this is also the most likely trigger for the market to begin pricing the 28 October Bank of Canada oil-assumption revision.

The single most important bilateral inflation event of the month, testing the +70bp core differential on which the pair's entire rate thesis rests. June saw CPI-trim fall to 1.80% and CPI-median to 1.90%, both below target and lower than May. A reversal above 2.0% would revive the Bank of Canada's hawkish option, compress the core differential from 70bp toward 50bp and force the 128,886-contract gross Canadian short to reconsider — all bearish for the pair.

catalysts.event: Section 338 tariffs take effect: 50% on Canadian motor vehicles, alcoholic beverages and dairy
catalysts.rationale: The dominant dated bilateral catalyst of the tactical window and the sharpest asymmetry in the pair. Three presidential proclamations of 20 July impose 50% ad valorem duties on roughly $20bn of Canadian exports, applying regardless of USMCA origin so the agreement provides no shelter, with no Canadian retaliation announced. The euro area by contrast secured a 15% ceiling effective 1 July with autos cut from 27.5% to 15%. Both economies depend on US demand but only one now has legal certainty, and the pair carries no premium for the difference.

catalysts.event: ECB Account of the 23 July 2026 monetary policy meeting
catalysts.rationale: Lagarde disclosed at the July press conference that some governors asked whether a hike should be considered, and the Account will document how many and how forcefully. Given the June Account recorded a unanimous hike justified under every projection scenario, a hawkish July Account would push September pricing from 77–83% toward 90% and widen the expected policy differential against a Bank of Canada with no equivalent disclosure inside the window.

catalysts.event: Canada Q2 2026 GDP by income and expenditure, plus June monthly GDP
catalysts.rationale: The definitive confirmation of Canada's growth inflection from 0.0% q/q in Q1 to approximately +0.8% in Q2, against a euro area that printed +0.4% q/q. A print at or above expectations, particularly with business investment contributing, would close the annual growth differential and validate the Bank of Canada's growth-has-resumed framing four days before its 2 September decision, the largest bearish-pair release of August.

The decisive input for the 10 September ECB decision and the other half of the core-differential test. July printed 2.9% headline with core at 2.5%, services 3.3% and energy 10.0%, all accelerating. A print at or above 2.9% locks in the September hike and holds the core differential over Canada at 70bp or wider; a print at or below 2.6% cuts hike odds below 55% and invalidates the tactical thesis outright.

catalysts.event: Bank of Canada interest rate announcement
catalysts.rationale: A hold at 2.25% is near-certain and fully priced; the information is entirely in the statement language. This meeting falls eight days before the ECB's, so Governing Council speaks first. If the statement acknowledges that oil has run $17–19 above the July MPR assumption, the market begins pricing the 28 October revision and the pair falls; if it repeats the look-through language unqualified, the euro's 10 September event runs unopposed.

catalysts.event: ECB Governing Council decision plus staff projections, hosted by the Bundesbank in Berlin
catalysts.rationale: The single most important dated event of the tactical horizon and the moment the policy differential mechanically opens from 0bp to +25bp. A 25bp hike to 2.50% is 77–83% priced, so the rate itself is a sell-the-fact; the larger information content is in the projections, which in June had HICP peaking at 3.4% in Q3–Q4 2026 with 2027 at 2.3%. An upward 2026 revision toward 3.2% with 2027 held at or above 2.3% extends the differential toward +50bp.

catalysts.event: Bank of Canada decision plus Monetary Policy Report
catalysts.rationale: The most underpriced scheduled event affecting this cross and the strategic inflection point. The July MPR assumed Brent near $75 in Q3-2026 settling to $70, WTI at $65 and WCS at $50 against actuals of $91.82 and $84.25 — a $17–19 inflationary gap the Bank must close, against its own published statement that a sustained oil increase would likely require a monetary policy response. A hawkish revision compresses the policy differential back toward zero.

catalysts.event: French Assemblée nationale solemn vote on the PLF 2027 as a whole
catalysts.rationale: The peak risk date of the European autumn and the largest identified euro-specific binary in this analysis, with no Canadian counterpart. If Article 49.3 is used without a pre-negotiated compromise a censure motion follows, and success means dissolution and snap legislative elections, assessed at 20–25%, taking OAT-Bund from 82bp toward 130bp and historically dragging the euro 1.0–1.5% lower independently of the ECB.

catalysts.event: Bank of Canada interest rate announcement (final 2026 decision)
catalysts.rationale: The meeting at which any 28 October MPR revision translates into action or explicit signalling. Consensus and the Bank's own Market Participants Survey have 2.25% at this date with no hike until March 2027; a hike or explicit hawkish signal would close the policy differential to 0bp or +25bp from a potential +50bp and remove the pair's central strategic support.

catalysts.event: ECB decision plus Eurosystem staff projections; European Council 17-18 December
catalysts.rationale: The market prices a 91.9% cumulative probability of an ECB deposit rate above 2.25% by this date, and the December Eurosystem round carries more weight than the September ECB-staff round because it extends the forecast horizon with national central bank input. A second delivered hike takes the differential to +50bp against a Bank of Canada that met eight days earlier.

catalysts.event: Full EU ban on Russian LNG imports takes effect
catalysts.rationale: A self-imposed euro-area supply cut landing in the same month as constrained Hormuz LNG transit and EU storage roughly ten percentage points behind the prior year — three independent supply constraints in one month. Under the framework's direction rules, LNG and gas price increases are −EUR and mildly +CAD, with Canada now a Pacific-basin LNG exporter, the clearest scheduled deterioration in the pair's terms-of-trade differential.

catalysts.event: French Conseil des ministres — PLF 2027 budget presentation
catalysts.rationale: Opens the euro area's dominant autumn risk narrative and the start of a sequence culminating in the 17 November solemn vote; a Bercy-commissioned report warns the deficit could reach 5.9% of GDP in 2027, and the market's reaction to the initial presentation sets the tone for OAT-Bund into the peak-risk period.

Tests the Merz coalition and lands in the same fortnight as the Google DMA compliance deadline, contributing to a densifying euro-area strategic-horizon event calendar that has no Canadian analogue in the same window.

signposts.indicator: Core inflation differential: euro-area HICPX minus Canada CPI-trim
signposts.current_level: +70bp in the euro's favour (HICPX 2.5% July 2026 flash vs CPI-trim 1.80% June 2026)
signposts.confirms_if: The differential holds at +70bp or wider, euro-area core at or above 2.5% and Canadian CPI-trim below 1.8%
signposts.invalidates_if: The differential compresses to +30bp or narrower
signposts.bilateral_importance: This is the single number that determines whether the ECB can out-tighten the Bank of Canada, and in a zero-carry pair the relative policy path is the only rate channel available — there is no carry to fall back on. Neither dossier frames it bilaterally, and the two releases fall within a fortnight of each other every month, making this a genuinely tradeable monthly signpost.

signposts.confirms_if: The gap narrows below +10 percentage points
signposts.invalidates_if: The gap widens beyond +30 percentage points

On absolute notional the two shorts are nearly identical (~$8.2bn and ~$7.4bn), which would imply no pair signal; proportionally the Canadian short is 3.9 times more crowded, the entire basis of the bearish Factor 4 reading.

signposts.current_level: +44bp in Canada's favour (GoC 3.59% vs Bund 3.15%, 30–31 July 2026)
signposts.bilateral_importance: This is the pair's cleanest single market-based read on the relative policy race, and it is genuinely anomalous — Canada pays 44bp more at ten years despite an identical 2.25% policy rate. It also isolates the bilateral signal from the US leg that contaminates both dossiers' own rate analysis: each dossier watches its spread to Treasuries, neither watches the spread to the other.

There is no Canadian analogue to French fiscal risk, so the spread is a one-sided input to the cross.

It must be watched against Canadian December pricing, currently near zero — the pair thesis requires divergence in the probabilities, not just a high euro one.
signposts.frequency: Continuous; check weekly and daily around data releases

assumptions: Spot, performance, 52-week range, range percentile, moving averages, trend regime, recent price action and realised volatility are taken exclusively from the provided Twelve Data daily OHLC series (390 observations, 9 June 2025 to 5 August 2026). Spot is the 5 August 2026 close of 1.62394, four sessions later than the 1 August valuation date carried in both dossiers (euro dossier 1.61690, Canadian dossier 1.61695 for the 31 July close); all pip and percentage calculations use 1.62394, and readers reconciling against the dossiers should note the pair has risen approximately 70 pips (0.43%) between the dossier snapshot and price-data spot.

Twenty-day realised volatility of approximately 3.5% annualised is computed from close-to-close log changes in the provided series; the series contains weekend/holiday flat prints that marginally suppress the computed figure toward understatement, and the mean daily true range of 0.35% of spot is offered as a corroborating measure.

All implied volatility, risk-reversal, vol-term-structure and option-barrier figures are estimates and are flagged throughout. No dated EUR/CAD implied volatility print was retrievable this cycle; the 1M estimate of 5.5–6.0 and 3M estimate of 6.0–6.5 are anchored on the euro dossier's own flagged estimate of 6.5 for EUR/CAD 3M. Risk-reversal direction is not asserted.

Forward points and outright forwards at 1M, 3M and 6M are COMPUTED from covered interest parity, not market-quoted, using €STR at 2.185% and CORRA at 2.31% as near-term anchors plus the priced ECB hike probabilities against a flat Bank of Canada path; the computation excludes cross-currency basis, which was not retrievable for either leg, so a basis error of a few basis points could change the sign at 3M though the qualitative conclusion is robust to that uncertainty.

Bilateral trade figures are taken directly from the injected IMF DOTS block for 2024 and are not re-estimated; the asymmetry between the two reporting directions reflects valuation basis and reporting convention differences and is stated rather than reconciled.

Bilateral valuation is constructed as a relative real-effective comparison using BIS real broad effective exchange rates (euro area 102.69, Canada 95.71), not an absolute PPP calculation; the BIS series available is short (30 monthly observations for the euro area, three months plus a year-ago comparator for Canada), so no historical percentile is asserted for either leg or for the cross.

Weight adjustments total zero on both horizons and are documented with specific bilateral justification for each, all within the framework's ±0.05 limit; the largest single adjustment is −0.04 to Factor 10 on both horizons (permitted for non-USD crosses).

Weighted scores are computed as stance score (Bullish +1, Neutral 0, Bearish −1) multiplied by confidence divided by 100, multiplied by the horizon weight, and summed; Neutral stances contribute exactly zero regardless of confidence. Score-to-conviction bands: absolute score below 0.10 maps to Neutral; 0.10–0.25 maps to conviction 2; 0.25–0.45 maps to conviction 3; above 0.45 maps to 4 or 5. The tactical score of +0.1022 clears the Neutral boundary by only 0.0022 and this is stated explicitly rather than presented as a robust Bullish reading.

Web-sourced support and resistance levels carry different vintages and are labelled accordingly; the 1.61728 pivot, 1.60918 support and 1.6230 resistance are dated 31 July 2026 (most current), while the 1.6175/1.6350/1.6500 range study is of an earlier vintage and treated as structural reference rather than current chart calls. Several technical services returned levels inconsistent with the price-data spot (1.48–1.59 range) and were discarded.

Scenario probabilities (50/25/25) follow the framework's standard structure and are subjective; individual invalidator probabilities are independent estimates and do not sum to 100% because the conditions are not mutually exclusive.

Both dossiers carry their own flagged data gaps that propagate into this analysis: the euro dossier could not retrieve the STOXX Europe 600 Banks index, the 3M EUR/USD cross-currency basis, the exact EUR/USD 25-delta risk reversal magnitude, or market-quoted forward points (3M implied volatility dated 13 May 2026); the Canadian dossier could not retrieve any volatility surface, cross-currency basis, or current WTI-WCS differential, and its moving averages are estimated from a sampled series.

The Canadian dossier discloses that the CFTC report dated 28 July 2026 shows the euro leveraged net short at 65,198 contracts against 819,806 lots of open interest (8.0%), deeper than the 21 July figure of 56,671 (7.1%) used as the cycle's source of truth; using the newer print would narrow the proportional positioning gap from +20.4 to +19.5 percentage points, a change that does not alter the Factor 4 conclusion in either direction. The 21 July figure is retained for consistency with the euro dossier.
